Neonates of the bushtailed caddisfly Sericostoma personatum emerge from eggs with a head-capsule width averaging 0.0234 cm [Lb = 0.0234 cm], a minute dimension that underscores the species' reliance on rapid early growth. The eggs themselves, which are spherical, exhibit a mean initial volume approximated by the formula for a sphere, which calculates to 0.0224 cm³  based on the typical egg diameter of roughly 3 to 4 mm. Female fecundity was assessed during a laboratory oviposition trial conducted at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], where a single female deposited a total of 351 eggs  across two distinct clutches within a single hour. The first clutch consisted of 162 ova, while the second, deposited shortly thereafter, contained 189 ova, demonstrating a rapid, bipartite laying strategy characteristic of some trichopterans. This reproductive output, when combined with the relatively small egg volume, suggests that females invest heavily in yolk provisioning to support a prolonged larval phase in cool freshwater habitats, a trade-off that shapes the species' overall life history.

The period required for embryonic development and larval hatching is strongly temperature-dependent. When eggs were incubated at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to the emergence of the first-instar larva, was determined to be 36 days [ab = 36 days]. This duration aligns with typical values for caddisflies developing under cool thermal regimes, reflecting slower metabolic rates at low temperatures. Once hatched, the larvae embark on an extended aquatic growth phase. At a higher rearing temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the time since birth at pupation, which marks the culmination of larval development, was recorded as 319 days . This lengthy larval period is a key life-history trait, reflecting the slow, steady accumulation of biomass in a detritivorous feeding niche within cool, lotic environments, where food processing and growth proceed at a leisurely pace.

During their final, seventh instar, the larvae of Sericostoma personatum reach their maximum dimensions before entering the pupal stage. The maximum head-capsule width observed in these late-instar larvae was 0.2 cm , a considerable increase from the neonatal measurement. Concurrently, the maximum larval length attained by these pre-pupal individuals was 1.2 cm , representing the peak somatic growth achieved during the aquatic larval phase. Following this period of maximal size, the prepupal larva constructs a pupal case and undergoes metamorphosis. The duration of the pupal stage itself was investigated at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], where the time since pupation at emergence, which encompasses the full histolysis and reorganisation into the adult form, was determined to be 40 days . This interval represents a crucial window of tissue remodelling before the final imago emerges.

Larval development in cooler waters significantly prolongs the pre-pupation period, an effect clearly documented under controlled photoperiod. Under a 16-hour light and 8-hour dark cycle, larval development at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] required 370 days  from birth to reach the pupation event. This interval, exceeding a full year, illustrates the profound effect of thermal conditions on growth rates in poikilotherms, where even modest temperature reductions can double the time needed to complete development. A further and even more pronounced extension was recorded at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], where the same developmental trajectory from hatching to pupation spanned 452 days . This substantial delay at near-freezing temperatures likely reflects a metabolic depression that slows feeding and tissue accretion, pushing the completion of the larval stage well into a second calendar year for individuals experiencing chronically cold headwaters, and constraining the species' geographic distribution to perennially cool streams.

Following its emergence from the pupal case, the imago of the bushtailed caddisfly leads a brief but crucial aerial existence dedicated to reproduction and dispersal. The lifespan of the adult imago, under controlled conditions at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], was documented as 21 days [am = 21 days]. This relatively short adult span, typically lasting between two and four weeks, appears to be a common strategy among non-feeding or minimally feeding adult aquatic insects, where stored larval reserves must sustain all flight, mate-location, and oviposition activities. In a comparative context, the extended larval development times observed at lower temperatures, such as the 370 days recorded at 10 °C, contrast sharply with the fleeting adult phase, underscoring a life history heavily invested in the aquatic, feeding larval stage. The seasonal timing of emergence, with the pupal stage requiring approximately 40 days at 14 °C, likely synchronises adult flight periods with optimal conditions for mating and egg deposition.
